usage_notes.narrative: In Chapter 2, Greenan establishes that the major 7th chord is the tonic chord of the Major Diatonic Series and functions as the resolution point of ii-V-I progressions. Its formula is Root-3-5-7, and the 3rd and 7th are the defining guide tones that must be targeted during improvisation.

In Chapter 4, Greenan states the formula for a major 7 chord is 'Root-3rd-5th-7th' and instructs the student that the 3rd and 7th are the guide tones -- the most important chord tones to use as melodic anchors over any maj7 chord. 'Continue to let the 3rds and 7ths of each chord be your guide.'

In Chapter 8, when moving from Cmaj7 to Cmin7, Greenan instructs the student to adjust only the b3 and b7 -- 'The only difference between a major 7 chord and a minor 7 chord is the minor has a b3 and a b7. Make this adjustment and you are good to go!' All other tones remain stable.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map assigns Ionian (the parent major scale, formula 1-2-3-4-5-6-7) as the prescribed pitch collection over maj7 chords functioning as tonic. For example, EbMAJ7 maps to Ionian and BbMAJ7 maps to Ionian in the Stella by Starlight analysis.

In Chapter 8, Greenan presents the bIImaj7 chord as a tritone substitution variant and chromatic passing chord replacing the V7 in a ii-V-I. 'The easiest way to think of this chord is a substitute for the V chord... bars 5-7 are a ii-V-I with a replacement for the V chord.' The bIImaj7 itself carries major quality, distinguishing it from a standard dominant tritone sub.

In Chapter 2, the minor 7th chord is established as the ii chord of jazz's most essential progression: 'there is no more important chord progression to know than the ii-V-I.' The formula is Root-b3-5-b7, and its 3rd and 7th are guide tones that resolve to the 3rd of the V7 chord via stepwise motion.

In Chapter 10, Greenan states a generalized rule: 'Where there is a V chord, you can almost always add a ii in front of it.' This means any min7 chord can be inserted before its companion dom7 to expand a V-I into a ii-V-I, and the student should deploy this expansion actively when navigating standards.

In Chapters 2 and 6, Greenan instructs that diatonic minor chords can and should be converted to dominant 7ths in jazz contexts. 'It is entirely normal and acceptable to turn minor chords in the diatonic series into dominant 7th chords.' The vi minor is the most frequently cited target for this conversion, generating secondary-dominant chains (VI7).

In Chapter 7, Greenan establishes that when a min7 chord functions as the ii chord or as a modal tonic (as in 'So What'), the Dorian mode (formula 1-2-b3-4-5-6-b7) is the prescribed pitch collection. D Dorian and Eb Dorian are the two operative modes for the entire tune. The student is instructed to treat Dorian not as a scale to run but as a 'note choice' inventory.

In Chapter 7, Greenan explicitly instructs the student to abandon guide-tone technique over modal min7 chords: 'Because So What is based on modal harmony, there is no need to identify the guide tones. This is because there is little to no harmonic movement actually happening.' Instead, modes serve as pitch collections and diatonic arpeggios connected by nearest chord tone replace guide-tone voice leading.

In Chapter 5, the min7 chord in the iv position (borrowed from parallel minor) is prescribed as a quick pivot into parallel minor tonality. Greenan offers concrete voicing options: 'The most basic way to approach it is with a V chord (Bb7) leading into the I. But often times, musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord... You can also turn that Abmin6 into a ii-V (Abmin7-Db7), or you can even just play a Db7.'

In Chapter 4, Greenan issues a direct avoidance rule for iv minor chords: 'Don't get too hung up on the iv minor chord. In your improvisation, you will simply want to consider the difference in the chord quality. Don't be playing major thirds or major 7ths!' The student must exclude natural 3 and natural 7 when improvising over any chord with minor quality.

In Chapter 11, Greenan names the backdoor ii-V pattern where a min7 chord precedes the bVII7 backdoor dominant: 'The ii chord is being added in front of the backdoor dominant. Therefore, the Bbmin7-Eb7 is really acting as a backdoor ii-V into the Fmaj7.' The student should recognize and deploy this min7 as the ii of the backdoor key area, not as a diatonic ii of the parent key.

In Chapter 2, Greenan establishes that the V chord 'is always dominant' -- both in major and minor diatonic series -- and that the ii-V-I is 'jazz's most essential harmonic pattern.' The dominant 7th formula is Root-3-5-b7, and its 3rd and 7th are guide tones that voice-lead to the resolution chord. 'The 7th of each chord resolves to the 3rd of the next chord.'

In Chapter 4, Greenan defines secondary dominants as 'dominant 7 chords that act as a V chord of a diatonic chord other than the tonic,' naming the process 'tonicization.' The student must read any dom7 appearing outside normal V function as a secondary dominant targeting the chord a fourth above it, and treat it with the same guide-tone and chord-tone tools used on the primary V.

In Chapters 2 and 6, Greenan instructs that a diatonic vi minor chord can be raised to a VI dominant 7th to generate cycling-fourths dominant chains. In 'Sweet Georgia Brown,' 'the vi minor is converted into a VI dominant,' and 'bars 1-13 are just a long cycle of dominant 7th chords resolving to the I chord.' The student should treat this conversion as idiomatic and unremarkable.

In Chapter 6, Greenan prescribes the Mixolydian scale as 'the primary melodic resource over dominant 7 chords.' 'The easiest way to think of a Mixolydian scale is a major scale with a b7. Formula: 1-2-3-4-5-6-b7.' The student is instructed to use it as a 'pitch collection' -- not a scale to run in order -- to generate melodic lines over any dom7 chord.

In Chapter 6, Greenan prescribes a specific chord-tone pattern exercise over cycling dominant 7th chords: 'The first and last lines begin with quarter note chord tones moving in ascending order: R-3rd-5th-b7. The second line descends in this order: R-b7-5th-3rd.' Each bar begins on a different chord tone to ensure the student can approach the arpeggio from any starting point.

In Chapter 10, Greenan instructs that any V7 chord is 'your secret weapon for resolving to a new key center': 'The V chord is always your secret weapon for resolving to a new key center.' When navigating multi-key standards, the student should insert or recognize a V7 at every tonal seam and use it as the modulatory fulcrum.

In Chapter 6, Greenan identifies a descending chromatic dominant approach as a reusable compositional device: 'We are just dealing with a series of chromatically descending dominant 7th chords that are targeting the VI7 chord.' The student should recognize this as a directed approach -- not random chromaticism -- and improvise with awareness of its resolution target.

In Chapter 11, Greenan formally defines the backdoor dominant as 'a dominant 7th chord that substitutes the V7 chord for a bVII7 chord approaching the I chord by a whole step. This works because the bVII7 has a lot of notes in common with an altered V7 chord. Example: Bb7-Cmaj7.' Mixolydian (the standard dom7 pitch collection) still applies, as it maps directly onto the bVII7's note content.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map for 'Stella by Starlight' prescribes Mixolydian over multiple dom7 chords in their straightforward dominant function (e.g., F7 maps to Mixolydian, Bb7 maps to Mixolydian, Ab7 maps to Mixolydian, Eb7 maps to Mixolydian). This confirms the default rule: unaltered dominant 7 = Mixolydian pitch collection.

In Chapter 6, Greenan warns against treating scales as mechanical exercises over dominant chords: 'The best way to think about the use of scales is "pitch collections." They aren't notes that are meant to be played in order, nor are they to be used solely to improvise.' The Mixolydian scale over dom7 is a note-choice map, not a fingering pattern to be played up and down.

In Chapter 9, Greenan teaches that a dominant 7(b9) chord can be represented by a rootless diminished seventh chord built on its 3rd: 'You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9).' The student should recognize that any dom7b9 shares four of its five chord tones with the diminished 7th built a major third above its root, making the substitution directly verifiable by ear.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map prescribes the Altered Scale over dom7(b9) chords in contexts of tension and chromatic approach (e.g., A7(b9) maps to Altered in the Stella analysis). Greenan introduces the Altered Scale as one of 'the ones you haven't seen before in this book' but confirms it as essential for Stella's chromatic harmonic landscape.

In Chapter 9, when improvising over the diminished passing chord that substitutes a VI7b9, Greenan instructs: 'Remember that it is being substituted for the VI7b9 chord, so any of those chord tones will serve you well.' The student should use the chord tones of the underlying dom7b9 (not just the diminished chord's own tones) as their primary note source.

In Chapter 11, Greenan introduces the Altered Scale as a required pitch collection for altered dominant contexts in 'Stella by Starlight,' flagging it as new vocabulary not seen in prior chapters. The Note Choice Map pairs Altered Scale with A7 chords in altered function throughout the form. The student must study this scale before attempting the Note Choice Map exercise.

In Chapter 11, Greenan introduces the Lydian Dominant as a new pitch collection essential for Stella's chromatic harmonic landscape alongside the Altered Scale. It is prescribed for dominant chords where the #11 (raised fourth / Lydian character) is implied or explicit. The student must learn it from the Note Choice Map before attempting the quarter-note solo exercise.

In Chapter 5, Greenan presents the half-diminished chord (min7b5) as the ii chord of the minor ii-V-I: 'If we look at a Gmin7(b5) and a C7(b9) as separate chords, they are confusing. But if we look at them as resolving to an Fmin7, then we have something functional to understand.' Formula: Root-b3-b5-b7. The student must always read min7b5 relationally -- through its resolution target -- rather than in isolation.

In Chapter 5, Greenan teaches a dual-analysis framework: the Gmin7(b5) in a ii-V of ii can simultaneously be read as 'the iiib5 (adding a b5 to the iii minor)' within the parent key, alongside VI7. 'A iiib5 is odd, but again, if we combine this understanding with the ii-V of ii concept everything ties together.' The student should maintain both readings simultaneously.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map for 'Stella by Starlight' assigns Locrian (formula 1-b2-b3-4-b5-b6-b7) as the prescribed pitch collection over every min7b5 chord in the form -- EMIN7(b5), and AMIN7(b5) all map to Locrian. This confirms Locrian as the default modal assignment for half-diminished chords.

In Chapter 11, Greenan defines the hybrid ii-V-I as using a min7b5 borrowed from the parallel minor: 'A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-I. The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key, but they resolve to the major I. Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7.' The student must recognize the minor-quality ii as the trigger for the surprise major resolution.

In Chapter 9, Greenan establishes the core rule for diminished 7th chords: 'F#dim7 chord is a substitute for the dominant VI7 chord... You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9).' The four chord tones of F#dim7 (F#-A-C-Eb) are identical to the upper four tones of D7(b9) (D-F#-A-C-Eb). The student should always reinterpret a dim7 as a rootless altered dominant one minor third below.

In Chapter 9, Greenan describes a dual function for the diminished passing chord: 'On a compositional level the F#dim7 is functioning as more than just a substitution. It's also creating a chromatic passing note, in this case the bass note, to connect the I chord with the ii chord.' The student should hear dim7 chords as performing simultaneous harmonic substitution and bass-line voice-leading duties.

In Chapter 9, Greenan prescribes the whole-half diminished scale as the pitch collection over diminished 7th chords: 'The intervallic formula for this scale is: W-H-W-H-W-H-W. The scale is based on alternating whole steps and half steps.' However, he cautions: 'I don't want you to play this scale verbatim when you are improvising... just playing the music rather than spending too much time getting bogged down in theory is more helpful.'

In Chapter 9, Greenan explicitly warns against running the whole-half diminished scale mechanically over dim7 chords: 'Of course, I don't want you to play this scale verbatim when you are improvising. That's why I think the best way to help you navigate these changes is to give you some musical ideas as a reference. In my experience, just playing the music rather than spending too much time getting bogged down in theory is more helpful.'

In Chapter 10, Greenan distinguishes the passing diminished (biii dim) from the substitution diminished: 'In this case, the biii diminished isn't necessarily replacing anything. Its primary job is to connect the iii chord to the ii chord chromatically.' The student must identify which role a dim7 plays -- substitution or connection -- before selecting note choices.

In Chapter 9, Greenan reveals that the bridge of 'Have You Met Miss Jones' is 'a series of ii-V-Is which our ears recognize. But the key centers are moving in a particular order. They are moving in 3rds. Bb to Gb is a descending major 3rd... Gb to D is a descending major 3rd... D to Gb is an ascending major 3rd.' The diminished logic that governs the A-section passes into a thirds-cycle architecture for the bridge.

In Chapter 5, Greenan offers the min6 chord as the primary voicing option for the minor iv function: 'often times, musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord.' The min6 is the first-choice voicing before the student considers expanding to a full ii-V (Abmin7-Db7) or simplifying to just the Db7.
